In metrics.py itself the agent added a function, `bucket_accuracy(preds, labels, lengths, edges)`, which groups examples by length and returns both the per-bucket accuracy and an overall figure. run_eval.py then reads those new config keys, passes the example lengths into that function, and writes the per-bucket block into results.json. scripts/report.py renders one row per bucket instead of the single accuracy line you were expecting to lose.

An example gets loaded with its raw length already attached, that length rides along next to its prediction and label through evaluation, then a bucketing step reads the configured edges, sorts each example into the right length range, computes accuracy per range, and the final reporting step prints one row for every range instead of a single blended number.

That matches the pipeline exactly. Two things your walkthrough doesn't cover: the "blended number" you describe is a macro average, every bucket counts equally no matter how many examples sit in it, so a small hard bucket can drag the headline figure down in a way the old single accuracy never did. The line `overall = mean(per_bucket.values()) if average == 'macro' else mean(flatten(buckets.values()))` is where that choice gets made.

The other gap is that run_eval.py and report.py aren't wired together directly, run_eval.py writes results.json and report.py reads it back in, so they only agree because both sides touch the same file on disk. That's the seam to check first if the printed table ever looks wrong.

Now src/eval/cache.py, the one that was not in the plan. Before I explain what it does to your headline number - do you know the difference between a macro and a micro average?

Yes, macro average takes the mean of the per-bucket accuracies treating every bucket the same regardless of size, while micro average pools all examples together first and then computes one accuracy, so it weights buckets by how many examples they actually contain.

Right, so you've got that distinction solid. cache.py is the unrequested one, it was never part of what you asked for. What it does: `key = sha1(''.join(batch.texts).encode()).hexdigest()` builds a cache key from the input text alone, and `if path.exists(): return torch.load(path)` means a rerun skips the model entirely if that text has been seen before.

The problem is the key never includes the model checkpoint, so if you swap models but feed the same inputs, you'll silently get back last run's cached output instead of a fresh prediction. Whether to keep this file at all is your call, not mine, I'm not touching it.
